passage.title: Muhammad Ali: The Greatest
paras: Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky, in the United States, in 1942. When he was twelve, his bicycle was stolen. He told a police officer, Joe Martin, that he wanted to fight the thief. Martin, who also trained young boxers, told him he had better learn to box first. Clay began training that week.

He was fast, confident and hard-working. In 1960, aged eighteen, he won the Olympic gold medal at the Games in Rome. In 1964 he became world heavyweight champion. Soon afterwards he announced that he had accepted Islam and took the name Muhammad Ali.

In 1967, at the height of his fame, Ali refused to be drafted into the army, saying his religion forbade him to fight in the war. The cost was immediate: his title was stripped, his licence to box was taken, and for three and a half years he could not fight. He did not give way. When the Supreme Court cleared his name in 1971, he returned to the ring, older but unbroken.

He won the world title again in 1974 and once more in 1978, becoming the first boxer to win the heavyweight championship three times. After he retired in 1981, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, an illness that affects movement and speech. He spent his later years supporting charities and speaking about peace and understanding.

In 1996 the world watched as Ali, his hands shaking, lit the Olympic flame in Atlanta. He died in 2016. He is remembered not only for his skill in the ring, but for standing by his beliefs when it cost him almost everything.
